scenario: Today’s generative recommendation papers separate training objectives from serving computation. BRIDGE restores item relationships behind SID identifiers, while LatentRec retains reasoning-training gains in a deployment mode that generates no reasoning. Other papers examine whether rewards concentrate recommendations on a few items, and whether factually grounded shopping answers yield workable plans.

papers.title: BRIDGE: Bridging the Semantic Quantization Gap for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Yatong Xiao, Mingjie Sun, Peng Wang, Wenjin Wu, Peng Jiang
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating Semantic IDs(SIDs), where an RQ-VAE quantizes each item into a hierarchical SID sequence that the decoder generates level by level. We identify an overlooked bottleneck in this paradigm: the Semantic Quantization Gap(SQG). Quantization derives SIDs from rich continuous signals, including codebook centroids, local neighborhood geometry, and level-wise entropy. However, the decoder receives only discrete identifiers and loses the semantic structure that shaped them. This mismatch manifests in three ways: a grounding gap, where the decoder lacks semantic anchors when target-side information is limited; a neighborhood gap, where token-level supervision discards inter-item similarity and exacerbates exposure bias; and a difficulty gap, where computation is allocated uniformly despite generation difficulty diminishing with depth. To bridge the SQG, we propose BRIDGE. Codebook-grounded latent reasoning injects frozen quantizer centroids as semantic anchors before SID generation. Privileged EMA self-distillation transfers neighborhood-aware knowledge from a teacher to an on-policy student, preserving inter-item geometry while mitigating exposure bias. Effort-aware recurrence allocates more computation to the challenging early levels and progressively reduces it with depth. Across three Amazon benchmarks, BRIDGE improves Recall@10 and NDCG@10 by 10.9% and 9.7% on average over the strongest baseline (up to 12.6% and 10.7%). In a one-week online A/B experiment on a large-scale e-commerce advertising platform with 5% traffic, BRIDGE improves eCPM by 0.65%.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval predicts the next item's Semantic ID (SID) one code at a time from user history, but ordinary next-code training checks only the probability assigned to the correct code. When that probability stays the same, redistributing the remaining probability among incorrect candidates does not change this cross-entropy loss. BRIDGE (the generative retrieval model studied here) also uses relationships between items to train the generator. In the reported Beauty ablation, the configuration with both added losses has 12.8% higher Recall@10 than the reported comparison configuration without those added losses.

papers.title: Do Recommenders Need to Think in Words? Latent Reasoning for Efficient LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.authors: Hongyang Su, Beibei Kong, Lei Cheng, Chengxiang Zhuo, Zang Li
papers.abstract: LLM-based recommender systems increasingly generate chain-of-thought (CoT) text before each item prediction to activate the LLM's reasoning capacity, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. We ask whether inference-time reasoning artifacts (textual or latent) can be replaced by training-time supervision alone, without loss of accuracy. We propose LatentRec, a framework for LLM-based generative recommendation that replaces inference-time reasoning artifacts with training-time per-step head supervision. LatentRec has three components. A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM's hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the ~14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss (PRL) supervises every intermediate state through the LLM's prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID. The trained LLM retains this accuracy without the module at inference, so the module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0-5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across three datasets, paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.
papers.summary: Generating reasoning before recommending items makes every request wait longer. Starting from user history during training, LatentRec repeatedly weights trainable token embeddings by similarity to the hidden state, averages them and feeds the result back into the same LLM. Each step predicts the target item’s first SID token, and the loss updates LoRA adapters; deployment removes the rollout module. On Beauty, compared with a fine-tuned textual-reasoning baseline, single-request latency fell from 10.80 seconds to 0.59 seconds and hit rate improved by a relative 5.0%. Multi-step supervision remains in the LoRA adapters, while serving generates items directly.

papers.title: Item Representations Matter: Bridging Hard Semantic IDs and Soft Prototype Mixtures for Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Vicente Balmaseda, Dongqi Fu, Jiarui Feng, Ren chen, Hanqing Zeng, Tianxin Wei, Yinglong Xia, Tianbao Yang, Hong Li
papers.abstract: Modern recommender systems rely on generative retrieval techniques to predict the next item either as discrete codes or as a continuous vector. On the one hand, Semantic IDs (SIDs) give discrete models shared parameters and pretrained semantic structure, but discretizing items into hard codes discards some information from the original content embeddings. On the other hand, continuous models avoid quantization, yet typically use flat item lookup tables with no explicit parameter tying across items. We ask whether a continuous recommender can introduce shared structure without making it a discrete bottleneck. We propose CAP-Mix, a flow recommender that represents each item as a soft mixture of shared prototypes plus an item-specific vector. The assignments, prototypes, and item vectors are trained jointly, and the soft representation is retained at inference. Pretrained information is optional: SID responsibilities can serve as a prior over assignments, while a full content embedding can initialize the item-specific vector without changing the initial flat table. In matched comparisons on three datasets, CAP-Mix improves over a flat table on the two sparse Amazon datasets and yields a small gain on Steam when trained without pretrained information. Given only an offline SID, it outperforms a hard table built from the same tokenizer by 4.45-14.90% in HR@5. Given the full content embedding, it matches or improves a strong flat table while hard assignments regress on the sparse Amazon datasets. Overall, averaged across six benchmarks, CAP-Mix improves HR@5 and NDCG@5 by 6.9% and 13.6% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each dataset and metric, while delivering 1.4-161x the inference throughput of the discrete baselines in our experiments.
papers.summary: Learning an independent embedding for every item limits information sharing for sparse items; assigning items permanently to SID groups loses differences within each group. CAP-Mix gives each item a learned weighted mixture of shared representative vectors plus its own vector. After training, these can be materialised as an item table, so serving need not repeat the mixture computation. With the same SIDs and backbone, HR@5 improved by a relative 4.45% to 14.90% over a hard-assignment table. The practical idea is to learn how much items share, instead of choosing only between fully independent vectors and fixed groups.

papers.title: What Gets Hacked in a Collaborative Reward for LLM Recommenders: The Part That Does Not Depend on the User
papers.authors: Zhuangsheng Li, Liang Dong, Yu Wu, Dailin Li, Yu Xia, Yunhan C. Zhang, Rui Cai, Yi Wu, Julian McAuley
papers.abstract: Collaborative-filtering (CF) scores provide graded, personalized rewards for training large language model (LLM) recommenders through reinforcement learning. However, these rewards can cause exposure collapse: even though the CF model itself produces diverse top recommendations across users, an LLM optimized with its rewards concentrates on fewer items. We decompose each score into an item-mean component, the item's average CF score across user histories, and a residual component, the current user's score deviation from the average. Through controlled interventions, we identify the item-mean component as a contributor to exposure collapse. Accordingly, we propose two reward corrections: per-item centering removes each item's estimated mean score, while per-item standardization further rescales the residual using its estimated standard deviation. Experiments on two datasets with two identifier schemes show that both corrections substantially improve catalog coverage and exposure evenness. Compared with training on the uncorrected CF reward, our corrections increase the number of distinct items ranked first across users by up to $9.8\times$, while maintaining comparable ranking accuracy. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM4Rec-CF-Bias-27EF/.
papers.summary: Using a collaborative-filtering model to reward generative recommendations can concentrate first-place results on the same few items. In the Beauty SID experiment, the number of distinct items recommended first across users fell from 1317 after SFT to 837. The paper subtracts each item’s average reward across users, retaining its deviation for the current user; the count recovered to 1830, but hit rate also declined. Part of the reward reflects an item’s broadly high scores rather than personalised matching. Separating these components changes recommendation concentration, without guaranteeing that accuracy comes at no cost.

papers.title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
papers.authors: Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua, Zijie Lei, Yan Xie, Jizhe Zhang, Lynn Lu, Delun Du, Sha Hua, Ren Mao, Ke Pan, Haomin Yu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon
papers.abstract: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.
papers.summary: A recommendation slate needs to account for items already selected, but rerunning the full model for every choice is expensive. MIS encodes candidates and display positions once, then feeds candidate, display-position and ordered selected-item representations into a lightweight head to choose the next item. Selection remains sequential without repeating full encoding. In a randomised online experiment, ranking-service CPU usage fell by 9.73% and watch time rose by 0.058%, while prediction-service CPU increased by 1.39%. Computation shifts toward reusable representations and cheaper sequential scoring, but percentages from the two services cannot be subtracted to establish total savings.

papers.title: PMRecBench: A Benchmark for Personalization in Recommendation Agents under Multimodal Queries
papers.authors: Xiaoyu Zhang, Yougang Lyu, Bin Wu, Sahan Bulathwela, Emine Yilmaz
papers.abstract: On Web platforms for shopping and entertainment, recommendation agents under multimodal queries aim to deliver personalized recommendations that satisfy users' visually specified requirements and reflect preferences inferred from user histories. However, existing personalized recommendation benchmarks use text-only queries, while multimodal ones assess query matching without evaluating personalization based on real user histories. We introduce the Personalized Multimodal Recommendation Benchmark (PMRecBench), the first benchmark to evaluate the personalization of recommendation agents under multimodal queries. It pairs 510 quality-controlled image-text queries across clothing and movies with the corresponding users' real histories. PMRecBench features two key designs: (1) queries derived from consistent behavioral patterns in real user records, with reference images and targets linked to actual interactions; and (2) challenging diagnostic pools with candidate items rated highly by the user but violating requirements, and items satisfying requirements but never rated highly, testing requirement understanding and preference following, respectively. Extensive experiments on diagnostic pools reveal a personalization imbalance in recommendation agents: relative to personalization signals alone, adding multimodal queries weakens preference following, even though the additional information about query requirements improves overall ranking performance. Further analysis links this decline in preference following to image interpretation, where agents can prioritize resemblance to reference images over evidence from user histories, and stronger commercial backbones alone fail to resolve this imbalance. This personalization imbalance highlights a central challenge for recommendation agents: improving ranking performance while preserving preference following when responding to multimodal user queries
papers.summary: A more specific shopping query with an image can improve compliance with the current request while reducing the influence of a user’s established preferences. PMRecBench evaluates these separately: the target meets the query and has a high user rating, while competitors meet the query but have low ratings or no past interaction; the test checks whether the target ranks above them. In Gemma’s multi-agent experiment, adding an image-text query compared with history-only input reduced this win share by 4.6 percentage points on clothing. Better overall ranking can therefore conceal weaker use of preference history. Adding multimodal input does not by itself establish better personalisation.

papers.title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines
papers.authors: Yuqin Dai, Zhanwei Zhang, Honghui Yang, Zhouheng Yao, Yueqi Zhang, Jingyu He, Chaoyang Shi, Fanding Wei, Boyuan Pan, Kai Xu, Yao Hu, Yongliang Shen
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.
papers.summary: A shopping assistant can understand requirements and state product facts correctly yet still propose an unworkable purchase plan. CARTBench fixes product evidence and evaluates replies along timestamped dialogue. Besides requirements and evidence, case-specific rubrics check whether advice supports a workable purchase decision. In the travel example, buying power adapters is deferred until the destination and charger specifications are checked. A rule violation or a required omission is a failure. Among replies passing all resolved need and evidence checks, 13.0% still failed a plan check. Factually accurate product claims therefore do not guarantee a workable recommendation.

papers.title: Generative Retrieval under Real-Time Supply Constraints in Local Commerce
papers.authors: Shaopeng Liang, Biao Zhang, Hongzhen Ye, Zeyang Hou, Ma Jiang, Jintao Tu, yunxi.hz, Zhijia Fang, Jianqiang Cao, Junxue Rao, Jia Jia
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval predicts semantic identifiers for candidate entities. In local retail and food delivery, candidates must also be serviceable for a particular user at a particular time. Location, weather, and traffic reshape merchant and product supply, so a catalog-valid identifier may be infeasible for the current request. Post-generation filtering removes such candidates only after beam capacity and inference computation have been spent. We study retrieval over an explicitly materialized, request-time supply snapshot, where short output sequences leave little opportunity to amortize online constraint preparation. Our RTP-LLM pipeline compiles eligible residual-quantization identifiers into a compressed sparse row prefix index, overlaps CPU compilation with model prefill, and shares the uploaded index across beams. Legal expansions retain original-model log probabilities, and constraint states follow selected beam parents. We formalize snapshot-relative identifier validity and distinguish it from entity-level eligibility and freshness. The implementation generates three-token merchant identifiers. Historical evidence covers T+1 daily-refresh catalog constraints and subsequent request-scoped serving evaluations. In one matched-beam daily-constraint case, filtered merchants decrease from 170 of 299 candidates to 29 of 299; residual distance filtering motivates request-specific constraints. A different-host comparison with 30,000 supplied entries reports a 0.6 ms service-side latency increment, while client measurements expose additional request costs. Captured requests from three geographic settings characterize behavior across supply sizes and output widths. These observations span development stages and measurement boundaries. They establish a practical implementation and identify bottlenecks, but do not establish compute savings at matched retrieval quality.
papers.summary: Local recommendations must generate items available for the particular request. Filtering only after generation can spend computation on items the user cannot buy. This paper compiles the request’s eligible items into a SID-prefix index and keeps only branches that can still reach an eligible item during decoding. CPU index preparation overlaps prefill. A request uses one fixed eligibility snapshot rather than continuously tracking inventory changes during decoding. The contribution is to enforce availability inside generation for location-dependent supply, while still requiring the request set and item identifiers to remain consistent.

papers.title: Multi-Teacher Reasoning Distillation for LLM Recommendation with Self-Exploration
papers.authors: Liangbo Ning, Siyuan Liang, Yi Zhou, Yifeng Zhang, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan, Dacheng Tao
papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented recommender systems (RecSys) enhance user preference modeling by generating reasoning trajectories over historical interactions before making recommendations. Knowledge distillation provides a practical paradigm for transferring such reasoning capabilities from powerful large language models to lightweight RecSys. However, existing methods typically rely on a single fixed teacher, remain constrained by the teacher knowledge ceiling, and indiscriminately distill teacher-generated trajectories without assessing their actual utility for downstream recommendation. To address these limitations, we propose MUSE (Multi-Teacher Utility-guided Selection with Self-Exploration), an adaptive reasoning distillation framework that jointly improves reasoning generation and reasoning utilization. MUSE first constructs a diverse reasoning pool using multiple teacher LLMs and progressively augments it via student self-exploration, enabling the student to leverage the strengths of different teachers and gradually explore reasoning strategies beyond teacher imitation. We then develop Rank-Gain Utility Assessment (RGUA), which evaluates each candidate according to the normalized full-catalog rank improvement of the ground-truth item and identifies the most and least recommendation-beneficial trajectories. Based on these utility-aware trajectory pairs, we introduce dual-level contrastive learning objectives that guide the student generator to prefer beneficial reasoning while training the recommendation encoder to more effectively exploit recommendation-relevant preference evidence. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: A fluent reasoning trace is not necessarily a useful training example for generative recommendation. MUSE compares how each trace changes the target item’s full-catalogue rank relative to using no reasoning. Training imitates the most helpful trace and requires its generation likelihood to exceed that of the least helpful trace. With the same model on VideoGames, HR@10 improved from 0.0844 with randomly selected traces to 0.1020. Target items are used to select training examples; serving does not ask a teacher to judge each trace again. Recommendation ranking supplies a more direct criterion for choosing reasoning data than the fluency of the explanation.

papers.title: Deliberate Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Haobo Zhang, Qiannan Zhu, Yutao Zhu, Zhicheng Dou
papers.abstract: Sequential recommenders are widely applied in real-world scenarios to model user preferences and behavior patterns based on user interactions. Recent advances in sequential recommendation enhance transformer-based models with latent reasoning to refine user representations by autoregressively generating intermediate reasoning vectors. However, exploring the optimal reasoning depth for diverse user histories remains challenging: existing methods typically employ a fixed number of reasoning steps for all users. This ``one-size-fits-all'' strategy often leads to suboptimal representation learning due to over-thinking in simple histories or under-thinking in complex ones. To address this issue, we propose DESRec, a deliberate latent reasoning framework that performs personalized latent reasoning to learn more informative reasoning states and enhance user modeling for sequential recommendation. Specifically, it designs a reasoning step selection module that identifies the optimal reasoning step for each user sequence during the training phase. Through a self-distillation mechanism, it compresses this most informative state into the final reasoning step, which serves as the final user representation for item ranking during inference. Moreover, it introduces a progressive preference extraction mechanism for personalized reasoning, which dynamically segments a user's history into a variable number of periods and summarizes each into a latent milestone representing the user's preference for that period. It will be used as the input of the subsequent reasoning. The number of milestones varies with the users' history, enabling a personalized reasoning over users' evolving interests. Extensive experimental results on six public datasets and four backbone recommenders demonstrate the superiority of DESRec over eight baseline models.
papers.summary: When a sequential recommender repeatedly applies the same computation block, an intermediate step can recommend better than the final one. During training, DESRec selects the intermediate state with highest cosine similarity to the known target item embedding, then teaches the final state its score distribution over items. Serving still runs a fixed number of steps and returns the final state. In the CDs SASRec experiment, relative NDCG loss from the best step to the last fell from 31.79% to 21.52%. This reduces deterioration in later steps without giving the deployed model advance knowledge of the best step or eliminating later computation.
